name: Uma Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on booking software for dental and physio clinics at a company of about seventy people. Mostly I build the screens receptionists use to move appointments around, and I fix what breaks when a clinic changes its opening hours. I like it when a receptionist tells me the new reminder texts cut their no-shows. What tires me out is the sprint planning, which takes a whole Monday morning.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm married to Ravi, who works in his family's hardware shop on the high street, and we rent a flat above a launderette two streets from his parents. We help pay for my younger sister's college fees, so our savings are under a month. The pay's lower than city jobs, but there are only a handful of software companies here, and we want to stay near family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's not so bad, is it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised and that it's good people kept their jobs. At work I'd say we should use the tools where they help, like test scripts. I don't post much online, but I'd share it in the family group chat with a sensible comment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief, but our money worries are the same as before. My sister's fees go up every year, and Ravi's shop has a quiet winter every year too. If the clinics cut back on software, we'd feel it, but they usually don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI tool now and then for tests and writing the help pages. I'd ask for a pay review, since I've been here four years. And Ravi and I would set aside a little each month, even if it's only enough for one month of rent by next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about AI, a bit worried about money. Money's always there in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which routine bits might AI take from you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing the help pages and the release notes, I think. Maybe a quarter of my week. That's fine, honestly, I'd rather do the screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your family think about your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum thinks I fix computers, which is close enough. My father-in-law asks me to fix the hardware shop's till every Sunday, and I don't mind, because that's how family works.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, and it's good people kept their **jobs**.
I'd suggest using AI tools where they help, like **test scripts**.
think: Our **money worries** stay the same, with my sister's fees and Ravi's quiet winters.
If **clinics cut back** on software we'd feel it, but they usually don't.
do: Keep using the **AI tool** now and then for tests and help pages.
Ask for a **pay review** after four years at the company.
Set aside a little each month to reach **one month's rent**.
feel: Mostly **calm** about AI, with **money worry** always in the background.
S0.quote: My father-in-law asks me to fix the hardware shop's till every Sunday, and I don't mind, because that's how family works.
fieldNote: Her money pressure comes from **family duties**, especially her sister's college fees.
She sees **clinic software** as fairly stable, which keeps the worry mild.
Family is woven into **everyday life**, from Sunday till repairs to the group chat.

steps.text: Keep using the AI tool for test scripts and help pages
Ask for a pay review after four years
Save towards one month's rent with Ravi by next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Booking and answering customers. That's exactly what our software does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people should work hard to keep up, not wait for someone to save them. At work I'd say let's learn the tools properly. In the family chat I'd tell the younger cousins to pick their courses carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think our product changes a lot. If an AI can book dental appointments by talking to patients, half of our booking screens aren't needed. The team would shrink, and I'm average, so I'd have to make myself useful fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I saw colleagues using the new tools well, I'd learn them properly, maybe in the first few months. I'd volunteer for the clinic setup work, visiting practices, because that's where the people side is. Ravi and I would cut takeaways and the gym, and put that towards savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Not panicking, but I'd lie awake doing sums some nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask family for help if things went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, before anything else. Ravi's parents would let us live upstairs from the shop if we needed. I'd rather that than any government help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gemma on support, who answers clinic calls all day. That's exactly what AI would take. She's a single mum, which makes it worse.

say: I'd say people should **work hard** to keep up, not wait to be saved.
I'd tell younger cousins to pick their **courses carefully**.
think: If AI books appointments by talking to patients, **half our screens** aren't needed.
The team shrinks, and I'm **average**, so I'd need to be useful fast.
do: Learn the **new tools** properly once colleagues prove them.
Volunteer for **clinic setup visits**, the people side of the job.
Cut takeaways and the gym to build **savings**.
S1.quote: If an AI can book dental appointments by talking to patients, half of our booking screens aren't needed.
fieldNote: She sees her own **product** being replaced, not just her tasks.
**Family before state** is her first instinct for support.
Worries for **Gemma**, a single mum on support, the most exposed colleague.

steps.text: Learn the new AI coding tools within a few months
Volunteer for clinic setup visits at local practices
Cut takeaways and the gym to save money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's frightening, honestly. Two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities will have to hold each other up. I'd go to the temple more, and I'd help organise support for people who lose work. I wouldn't want the government running everyone's lives, but I'd accept help if it came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job is gone. If AI can do any thinking work, it can run a booking system, write the code and answer the receptionist. The robots coming later doesn't help me, because nothing I do is with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd talk to Ravi about me working in the hardware shop, because shops still need someone behind the counter for a few years. We'd move in above the shop with his parents to save rent. And I'd stop sending money for my sister's fees, which would break my heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and guilty about my sister. For the first time I'd feel like I can't hold my family up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That she has to work part-time to pay her own fees. She's nineteen; she can do it. I'd still feel like I let her down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long could the hardware shop carry you both?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few years, maybe until the robots come in 2031. After that, I don't know. People might still want advice on which screws to buy from someone who knows them.

say: I'd say **families and communities** will have to hold each other up.
I'd accept **government help** if it came, but wouldn't want it running our lives.
think: My job is **gone**, because AI can run the booking system end to end.
Nothing I do is with **my hands**, so the robot delay doesn't help.
do: Ask Ravi about working in the **hardware shop** straight away.
Move in **above the shop** with his parents to save rent.
feel: **Scared**, and **guilty** about letting her sister down.
S2.quote: For the first time I'd feel like I can't hold my family up.
fieldNote: Her fallback is **family**: the shop and a home above it.
Stopping her sister's fees is the **hardest choice** she names.
She'd accept state help only **reluctantly**, fitting her traditional views.

steps.text: Work behind the counter in Ravi's family hardware shop
Move into the flat above the shop with Ravi's parents
Stop paying her sister's college fees
Lean on the temple community for help finding work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare, so people should get on with it. I'd tell the cousins to learn practical skills alongside their degrees. At work I'd ask managers to be honest about the plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I get three years before my job thins out. Then I need something hands-on that robots won't do until 2034. I keep thinking about dental nursing, because I already know clinics and the people in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time dental nursing course after two years, once I see what's happening at work. I'd keep the software job until then and save, aiming for two months. My sister would finish college, because there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it feels possible. Five years is enough to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really switch from software to dental nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, yes. I've watched those nurses for four years from the booking side. Dental nursing is hard work, but it's real work, and patients want a person in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ravi think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say do whatever keeps us near family. He's never wanted to move away. That's the same thing I want.

say: I'd say there's **time to prepare**, so people should get on with it.
I'd tell cousins to learn **practical skills** alongside their degrees.
think: I get **three years** before my job thins out.
**Dental nursing** appeals because I already know clinics and the people in them.
do: Start a part-time **dental nursing** course after two years.
Keep the software job and save **two months** of rent.
Keep paying my sister's fees so she **finishes college**.
S3.quote: Dental nursing is hard work, but it's real work, and patients want a person in the room.
fieldNote: Her switch to **dental nursing** grows out of years on the booking side.
With five years, her **sister's fees** survive.
Staying **near family** guides every choice she and Ravi make.

steps.text: Start a part-time dental nursing course in two years
Save two months of rent before the course
Keep the booking software job until the switch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That sounds almost normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone to plan, so there's no excuse. I'd tell the younger ones to learn a trade and keep their faith. I'd stay away from the arguments online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm fine for a good while. My job changes, but I'd still be doing something in clinic software for five or six years. After that I'd need a plan, and I'd have time to make one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new tools as the team does, without rushing. We'd try for a baby in the next couple of years, as we planned. I'd save more steadily and maybe think about dental nursing later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. It's a worry for later, not for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about having children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Ten years is too long to wait on having children; my parents had nothing, and they managed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get comfortable and not act in time. Ravi's the same. Our parents would push us, though.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough for anyone to plan, so there's **no excuse**.
I'd tell the younger ones to **learn a trade** and keep their faith.
think: I'd still work in **clinic software** for five or six years.
After that I'd need a plan, and I'd have **time** to make one.
do: Learn **new tools** as the team does, without rushing.
Try for a **baby** in the next couple of years.
S4.quote: Ten years is too long to wait on having children; my parents had nothing, and they managed.
fieldNote: With a decade her **own job** feels safe for now, so she's uneasy.
**Family plans** go ahead, grounded in her parents' story.
She worries about **getting comfortable**, but trusts family to push.

steps.text: Learn the new AI coding tools as the team adopts them
Try for a baby with Ravi within two years
Save a steady amount from each pay cheque

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I couldn't keep helping my sister and we'd have to move in with Ravi's parents. What would help is cheap evening courses for hands-on jobs like dental nursing, and lower taxes for family shops like Ravi's.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family. People talk about jobs like we're all on our own. Most people I know would get through AI because of their family, not their employer.

headlineQuote: Most people I know would get through AI because of their family, not their employer.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old** developer building booking screens for dental and physio clinics.
She's married to Ravi, who works in his **family's hardware shop**, and helps pay her sister's fees.
She uses AI **now and then** and waits for colleagues before committing.
She'd lean on **family** first, and sees dental nursing as her hands-on fallback.
Her mood moves from uneasy to **alarmed** when AGI arrives in two years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would end her sister's fees and their own flat.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **evening courses** for hands-on jobs like dental nursing.
**Lower taxes** for family shops like Ravi's.
